lesson_title: The Duvet Trick That Saves Lives
hook_text: An egg thrown at a wall smashes. The same egg, thrown just as hard at a duvet, survives. Why?
clip_script: Hurl an egg at a brick wall and it is instantly scrambled. Hurl the same egg, just as fast, at a thick duvet on the washing line — it sinks in, slows down, and survives. Same egg, same speed, same change in momentum. So what saved it? Time. Against the brick, all that momentum is destroyed in a millisecond, and forcing the change into a sliver of time demands a savage force. The duvet yields, and the identical change unfolds across half a second instead. Same total change, hundreds of times more time, hundreds of times less force — and eggshell can handle a small force. Now look around, because engineers built the world out of this trick. An airbag is a duvet for your face. A crumple zone is a car agreeing to be wrecked slowly so you are not. The gravel run-off bed on a mountain pass is a duvet the length of a rugby field. A cricketer riding a fast catch backwards, a gymnast folding at the knees — everyone is buying time to shrink the force. That is the impulse-momentum theorem, the first big equation of the final physics year: force times time equals change in momentum. The change is fixed. Stretch the time, and the force has nowhere to go but down.
visual_style: Split screen of an egg meeting brick and an egg sinking into a hanging duvet, with a force arrow shrinking as a timer stretches; rapid cuts to an airbag inflating, a crumple zone folding, and gravel spraying in a run-off bed.
mood: Playful and mischievous, then suddenly serious — physics that saves lives.
pacing: Sharp smash to open, slow-motion duvet catch, rapid-fire montage of safety devices, calm one-line close.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and make momentum your most dependable physics topic.
